summary: Describes how the IESG handles documents submitted for RFC publication from the Independent Submission and IRTF streams. It updates procedures from RFC 2026 and RFC 3710. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Some documents arrive at the RFC editor from outside the main working groups. This explains how the IESG checks them to make sure they do not conflict with the main work.

subtitle: How the IESG reviews documents from outside the main IETF track

tldr.problem: Documents submitted for RFC publication from the Independent Submission and IRTF streams need IESG review to check for conflicts with IETF work, but the scope and process for this review was unclear.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG performs a focused review for conflicts (not technical merit), concluding with one of five outcomes ranging from no conflict to cases where IETF review is required. The RFC also defines a dispute resolution process.
tldr.outcome: The IETF community has clear procedures for managing non-IETF-stream documents while maintaining standards integrity. This document obsoletes RFC 3932 and updates RFC 2026 and RFC 3710.

today: RFC 5742 is the current standard for how the IESG reviews Independent Submission and IRTF stream documents. It has not been superseded or updated.

sections.title: Handling Documents from Outside the IETF Stream
sections.content:
RFC 4844 defines four publication streams for Internet RFCs: the IETF stream, the IAB stream, the IRTF stream, and the Independent Submission stream. Most protocol standards come from the IETF stream, which involves working groups and full community review.

However, the RFC Editor accepts submissions from individuals and research groups outside this path. Before the IETF changed its procedures in 2004, IESG members spent considerable time doing in-depth technical reviews of all Independent Submission documents, which created delays.

In 2004, the IETF switched to a conflict review model: the IESG now focuses only on checking whether a submission conflicts with ongoing IETF work, not on evaluating its technical merit. Technical review is the RFC Editor's responsibility (for Independent Submissions) or the IRSG's responsibility (for IRTF submissions).
sections.plainLanguage: Some RFCs come from people outside the main IETF groups. The IETF checks that these documents do not interfere with its own work, but does not vet every detail.

sections.title: History of the Review Process
sections.content:
Before RFC 3932 (published 2004), the IESG reviewed all Independent Submission documents for technical content and tried to steer authors toward working groups or suggest major revisions. This consumed significant IESG resources and often caused long delays.

RFC 3932 introduced the conflict review model in 2004. For the first time, the IRTF also established formal procedures for document publication, and the IRTF stream documents also became subject to IESG conflict review.

This RFC updates RFC 3932 for consistency with IRTF procedures and reflects changes to RFC headers and boilerplate made by the RFC Editor and IAB. It clarifies that the same conflict-review process applies to both Independent Submission and IRTF stream documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, the IETF spent lots of time checking all outside documents carefully. Now it just checks that they do not block IETF work.

sections.title: What IESG Conflict Review Covers
sections.content:
The RFC Editor or IRTF requests that the IESG review a document for conflicts with the standards process or work done in the IETF community. The review is not a technical review; it does not judge the quality, correctness, or usefulness of the work.

The IESG typically completes the review within four weeks. If a possible conflict is found, the IESG may contact relevant working groups, working group chairs, or IANA experts to get outside opinions.

If no conflict is found, the RFC Editor (for Independent Submissions) or IRSG (for IRTF submissions) is responsible for deciding whether the document has merit and should be published.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF checks that the document does not step on any toes. If it is okay, someone else decides whether it is worth publishing.

sections.title: Five Possible Conclusions from IESG Review
sections.content:
The IESG review results in one of five conclusions:

  1. No conflict: The document does not conflict with IETF work. The RFC Editor or IRSG may proceed with technical review and publication decisions.
  2. Related but not harmful: The work is related to something a working group is doing, but this relationship does not prevent publication. The IESG may request an IESG note explaining the relationship.
  3. Potential disruption: Publication could potentially disrupt IETF work in a specific working group. The IESG recommends not publishing at this time.
  4. Violates IETF procedures: The document violates IETF procedures for something (such as registering a URI scheme) and should not be published without full IETF review and IESG approval.
  5. Requires protocol review: The document proposes changes or extensions to an IETF protocol that may be detrimental to the protocol's use and requires IETF review.

In cases 4 and 5, the IESG offers the author the chance to resubmit as an AD-sponsored individual submission subject to full IETF review. This does not guarantee publication but does ensure IETF consideration.
sections.plainLanguage: The check can say: okay to go ahead, related but fine, wait a bit, this violates the rules, or this needs IETF approval.

sections.title: IESG Notes and How Disputes Are Resolved
sections.content:
In cases where the relationship of a document to the IETF standards process might be unclear, the IESG may request the inclusion of an IESG note in the published RFC. This note clarifies the document's status and relationship to IETF work, typically with pointers to related RFCs.

If the RFC Editor or IRSG disagrees with the content of a requested IESG note, they must provide clear concerns to the IESG before proceeding without it. The RFC Editor or IRSG may propose alternate wording.

If disagreement remains, an informal dialogue occurs, lasting up to six weeks. The IESG can reaffirm, modify, or withdraw the requested note. If the dialogue fails and the RFC Editor or IRSG intends to publish without the note, they may ask the IAB for arbitration. The IAB may accept or decline; if it accepts, the IAB's decision about the note is binding.
sections.plainLanguage: If the IETF says 'we should add a note explaining this', but the publisher disagrees, they can argue about it. A referee (the IAB) can make a final call.

sections.title: When Publication Might Be Delayed or Recommended Against
sections.content:
The RFC lists two example scenarios where the IESG might recommend against publication:

Rejected alternative bypass: A working group rejects a proposed solution to a problem and continues with its own approach. A participant then asks to publish the rejected solution as an Independent Submission, potentially giving the rejected alternative an RFC number before the WG's chosen solution is published. This could confuse the community about which solution the IETF adopted. Example: RFC 2522 (Photuris) was published after IKE (RFC 2409) to avoid this confusion.

Inappropriate reuse of reserved bits: In 2003, a proposal wanted to reuse reserved bits in the IP header for a different purpose without IANA approval. The IESG concluded that implementations risked hard-to-debug interoperability problems and recommended against publication. The RFC Editor accepted the recommendation.

The RFC notes that rejecting publication does not prevent these documents from being available through other channels; it only addresses their placement in the RFC series.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives examples of when waiting makes sense: when an alternative is being published soon anyway, or when reusing reserved bits could cause problems.
